text: I was also think this feature sounds a little but gimmicky, but just this morning I had a situation where it would have been nice. I do some setting for rope climbing and we use a petzl hand ascender and the Petzl rig to move up and down ropes how climbers would use an ascender and grigri. Every time you step up on the ascender and pull in slack, you can only pull in the amount of rope between the ascender and Rig. Today I was training a new person on our systems who is very short which limited how high they could push the ascender. Because the rig is so tall and we had it connected by a large carabiner there was not much rope between the Rig and the Ascender, this severely limited how much they could actually move up the rope each step. If I had this device, I would have opted to connect it directly to their harness without a carabiner, and it would have allowed them to ascend more efficiently, getting an extra few inches each step. It also would mean the device is just lower and more out of the way when trying to manipulate holds on the wall. This feature seems niche when thinking about the climbing world, but in my opinion it seems like this device was created with the ideas and mentality of the rope access world which has different needs, optimized for how climbers want a device to work. Just my two cents. Edit: I personally do not see this as something that will "replace the Grigri" but because it has rope access certifications it is an awesome option for users like gyms or maybe rescue teams who want the functionality of a Grigri along with professional certifications. Instead of gym setting teams having both Rigs and Grigri’s, they could just have this and only train on one device.

text: Well, everybody's always glad when YOU join the party, Captain Buzzkill. In actual fact, climbing gear recalls are LEAST likely to occur when brand new models hit the market, because gear makers usually invest a considerable amount of extra quality-control into new launches. New gear designs often take years to bring into production, with lots of fixed time delays for mandatory certification procedures -- so there's rarely any reason for a gear maker to rush. Recall issues are far more common with mature products, later in their lifecycle, when gear companies make changes to their production process. New suppliers, new assembly operations, etc are the most common source of recall-worthy quality control failures. Now, there are plenty of new products that just don't go over well with the public, for various reasons -- perfectly safe & well made, but just not to the majority's preferences. But a more thoughtful person than you might have realized that different folks have different preferences. It's impossible to find what works best for each of us without individually exploring the available options. I'm just glad that most folks aren't as paralyzed by fear of the unknown as you seem to be... What a terrible world THAT would be!
